Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Of the total prosecuted, 628 had arrived by small boat. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Immigration and asylum More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022 Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular means Diane Taylor Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.54 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 1,100 people, including survivors of torture and trafficking, have been convicted of illegally arriving in the UK since 2022, according to freedom of information data. The Home Office introduced the offence of illegal arrival in 2022 in a bid to deter those planning to come to the UK by small boat or by other irregular means such as lorries. The decision was widely condemned at the time because the refugee convention states that those seeking sanctuary should not be criminalised for the way they travel, as they often do not have the option to move legally from an unsafe country to a safe one. FoI data obtained from the Home Office by the criminologist Dr Victoria Taylor, a research fellow at the University of Manchester, reveals 1,109 people were prosecuted for illegal arrival between July 2022 and January 2026. The data shows 628 arrived on a small boat, 296 of whom were captured on surveillance drone footage steering a dinghy. Others had previous immigration history in the UK. Just 12 people have been convicted of the separate offence of facilitation, after steering the dinghies they arrived on. It is harder for the Home Office and Crown Prosecution Service to secure evidence that people on a dinghy were involved in organising a journey across the Channel than to prosecute them for illegal arrival. Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire Read more People have been identified as having their “hand on the tiller” for many reasons, including having boating experience, steering in return for discounted passage, taking it in turns, or being under duress. In one illegal arrival case, the Home Office settled a judicial review relating to a trafficking survivor from South Sudan who was forced at gunpoint to pilot a small boat. Officials have now agreed to ensure greater protection for trafficking victims in these cases. Emily Soothill, partner at Deighton Pierce Glynn, who represented the man, said: “Unfortunately it is clear from our client’s case that potential victims of trafficking are regularly being convicted for illegal arrival and imprisoned for many months. The concessions made in our client’s case underline the need for a robust and consistent application of the UK’s modern slavery framework to prevent survivors of trafficking from being wrongly treated as criminals.” Some of those convicted of the various offences were survivors of torture and trafficking, and there were at least 30 age disputed children among them, 19 of whom had spent time in adult prisons. The organisation Captain Support UK has worked with hundreds of people imprisoned in illegal arrival cases, all of whom sought asylum in the UK in the hours before they were arrested. A spokesperson said: “We see first-hand the negative impact these prosecutions have on people and their families. We urgently call on the government to stop imprisoning people on the move. No one should be put in prison for seeking safety and a better life.” Taylor said: “The process of who is selected for prosecution is arbitrary and cruel.” She added that the most of those imprisoned for illegal arrival since 2022 had claimed asylum in the hours before they were arrested. Many have been granted asylum since their release or have been recognised as victims of trafficking, or both. “There are serious questions about the compatibility of these prosecutions with the refugee convention, which was drafted to prevent states from penalising refugees for how they seek safety. There is no evidence to support the government’s claims that these prosecutions will ‘deter’ people from attempting to cross the Channel,” Taylor said. The Home Office has been approached for comment. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Nationals leader Matt Canavan and opposition leader Angus Taylor say they will support a One Nation bill to prevent Australians linked to overseas terrorist groups from returning to Australia Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen Nationals leader Matt Canavan and opposition leader Angus Taylor say they will support a One Nation bill to prevent Australians linked to overseas terrorist groups from returning to Australia Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Australian politics Coalition to back One Nation policy barring overseas Australians with terrorist links from returning home Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan will support Pauline Hanson’s migration bill despite vowing to fight her rightwing party Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Coalition will back a plan by Pauline Hanson to prevent Australian citizens with links to overseas terrorist groups from returning home, significantly elevating One Nation’s policy prescriptions on matters of national security. Despite pledging to fight Hanson’s insurgent rightwing movement amid collapsing support for their own parties, the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, both signalled support for One Nation ’s bill to bar the return of foreign fighters ahead of its introduction to the Senate on Wednesday. Key members of Taylor’s frontbench, including the shadow foreign minister, Ted O’Brien, and the shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, have offered to work with Hanson on her bill. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We’ll work with them on that legislation, it is important we get it right,” Duniam said. “We’d love to see it go off to a Senate committee to make sure that people who know a little more than we in the Senate know, legal experts to make sure it is robust. “We want to shut the door on terrorists, we’ve been trying for years to do this.” Even with the Coalition’s support, the One Nation bill won’t be debated in the House of Representatives without Labor facilitating its progress. Such a move would be extremely unlikely, after the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said last month that Hanson’s plan “would last about 30 seconds in the high court”. 6:27 Barnaby Joyce suggests One Nation could welcome some refugees while barring other migrants – video But the Coalition’s support is significant, not least because national security is a traditional political strength for the Liberal and National parties. Hanson’s bill would allow Australian passports to be cancelled more easily and create new penalties for anyone assisting the return of people with links to terrorist groups. It would establish a new “foreign terrorist fighter exclusion order” regime, imposed by the federal court at the request of the home affairs minister. The Albanese government used existing exclusion orders to temporarily bar one Australian woman linked to Islamic State from returning, but conceded it did not have powers to permanently block citizens from entering the country. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Pauline Hanson echoes Trump as she lashes out about ‘fake news’ reporting on lavish London hotel Read more Burke has argued Australian citizens blocked from returning could be more dangerous overseas and outside the reach of security agencies, while also noting countries have responsibilities to other nations to deal with their own citizens. Despite promising to fight Hanson’s rise in the polls , Canavan on Tuesday said the Nationals would work with One Nation on the bill. “I’m happy to work with anyone in parliament to make our country better, in this case, safer and more secure. “We have, for a long time, sought to ensure that those people who are subscribing to and supporting violent ideologies pay a penalty in this country, potentially lose rights or are deported.” Canavan said the Coalition had wanted to make similar moves as far back as the Abbott government. “We’ve indicated, and I know Angus has indicated, to Senator Hanson that we’re happy to work with her on her bill this week.” Taylor has a separate plan to target charities and community groups working to help Australians linked to terrorist groups return home. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/21/mol-.text: Menü Kereső Szoftverfrissítéssel küzd a BKK a fantombubik ellen Belföld Legfontosabb Fotó: Huszti István / Telex Tenczer Gábor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A kerékpárok zárrendszeréhez kapcsolódó szoftverfrissítést kapott a MOL Bubi flotta, hogy a helyadatokat pontosabban kezeljék a bringák, tájékoztatta a BKK lapunkat. Az utóbbi időben olvasóink tapasztalata alapján megsokasodtak az úgynevezett „fantombiciklik”, vagyis megnőtt az olyan esetek száma, amikor az alkalmazásban megjelenő pozíció nem egyezik a kerékpár tényleges helyével. A tájékoztatás szerint a frissítés jelenleg is zajlik, naponta újabb kerékpárok kapják meg az új szoftvert, a flotta több mint 90 százalékán már telepítve van. Emellett a BKK válasza szerint az alkalmazásban megjelent egy új fejlesztés is, ami azokat a helyzeteket kezeli, amikor a kerékpár valójában az állomáson található, a rendszer azonban pontatlan helyadat miatt máshová helyezi a térképen. Az alkalmazásfrissítés automatikusan megtörténik azoknál a felhasználóknál, akik korábban ezt beállították, de manuálisan is van mód frissíteni az applikációt. Legutóbb arról számoltunk be, hogy a hiányzó állomások, összekevert lerakópontok miatt nincs könnyű helyzetben, aki szeretné átlátni a megújult budapesti közbringarendszert. Erre a cikkünkre írt Péter, aki szerint nemcsak a felhasználók nem tudják gyakran, hova is kell letenni a bicikliket, hanem gyakran köszönő viszonyban nincs a valósággal a helyadat sem, ami az alkalmazásban látszik a kerékpárról. Mi is tapasztaltunk már olyat, hogy mind a biciklik helyzetmeghatározása, mind az azonosítása bizonytalan. Nemcsak fantombiciklik vannak a különböző helyeken, hanem az állomáson sem lehet felvenni biciklit, ami azt hiszi magáról, hogy teljesen máshol van. Ilyen hibákat egyébként az év elején régi Bubi-biciklikkel kibővült Manfréd is produkált az első hetekben. A BKK szerint a MOL Bubi 3.0 jelenleg az indulási időszakát éli, ezért a rendszer működését a BKK és szolgáltatója folyamatosan monitorozza és a valós használati tapasztalatok alapján finomhangolja. A visszajelzések alapján ismert probléma, hogy egyes esetekben a kerékpárok alkalmazásban megjelenített helyzete eltérhet a valós helyzettől, illetve előfordulhat, hogy egy kerékpár a rendszer szerint nem ott található, ahol a felhasználó ténylegesen látja. A hiba hátterében több tényező áll, részben a kerékpárok helymeghatározásának pontossága, részben az állomások digitális határainak finomhangolása. A probléma megoldásán a BKK a szolgáltatóval közösen több területen is dolgozik. A MOL Bubi 3.0 rendszerében az állomások virtuális határainak finomhangolása is folyamatos, tette hozzá a BKK. A tapasztalatok alapján a szolgáltató rendszeresen felülvizsgálja és szükség esetén módosítja ezeket a beállításokat annak érdekében, hogy a rendszer minél pontosabban érzékelje a kerékpárok helyzetét és a parkolás helyét. Fontosnak tartják ugyanakkor, hogy a helymeghatározás pontosságát a városi környezet is befolyásolhatja. A magas épületek, a rendelkezésre álló hálózati kapcsolatok vagy más környezeti tényezők időnként ronthatják a GPS-adatok pontosságát. A most bevezetett fejlesztésektől ugyanakkor jelentős javulást vár a BKK, miközben a rendszer további finomhangolása is folyamatosan zajlik. A következő hetekben már pontosabb adatok állhatnak rendelkezésre arról, hogy az eddigi beavatkozások milyen mértékben javították a helymeghatározás pontosságát. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36d.text: Image source, Crown copyright Image caption, Royal Marines from 45 Commando were on Exercise Saber Strike in Latvia in 2018 when they were allegedly exposed to asbestos By Rebecca Ricks BBC South West Investigations Published 20 August 2026 A group of 256 Royal Marines and soldiers, who claimed the Ministry of Defence (MoD) had "knowingly" exposed them to asbestos, have settled out of court for an undisclosed sum. Court proceedings were issued against the MoD in February 2024 by the group, from Plymouth and Scotland, claiming their employer had breached the Human Rights Act. The potential exposure was said to have taken place in Latvia in 2018 and 2019 over two exercises , with a sample collected by a marine at the time found to contain asbestos. The MoD, which did not accept liability, said action had been taken to "prevent similar issues arising in the future" and further use of the non-MoD training site had been prohibited. Image caption, Royal Marines took part in two military exercises in Latvia in 2018 and 2019 at an abandoned former Soviet town called Skrunda-1 An MoD spokesperson added: "Our people make extraordinary sacrifices to keep our country safe, often operating in challenging environments around the world, and their health, safety and wellbeing will always be our highest priority." Former Plymouth Royal Marine Edward Hill, who first logged the case in 2019, said while he was disappointed there had been "no accountability" the group were overall "happy with the settlement". "We now have to live our lives not knowing whether we're going to contract an asbestos-related illness," he said. Another former Royal Marine previously told the BBC it felt like someone had "potentially handed me an unnecessary death sentence". The claim for compensation related to two exercises, Saber Strike 18 (SS18) and Baltic Protector 19 (BP19), which took place in the Latvian base called Skrunda-1 in 2018 and 2019. It involved former and serving marines from Plymouth's 30 Commando, Arbroath's 45 Commando and attached Army soldiers. Hill, who was on BP19 with 30 Commando, expressed concern over the dust in a disused building at Skrunda-1 they were being asked to sleep in. He asked a superior if the group could sleep outside in a tent instead but was refused due to safety concerns and claims they were later told to lay down boards to stop the dust from being disturbed. Hill then took it upon himself to collect a 2kg (4lb) sample from where they slept. The firm which tested the sample told the BBC it contained Chrysotile fibre, a white loose asbestos usually found in pipe insulation or corrugated roofs. Part of the group's claim was the MoD knew asbestos was present at Skrunda-1 before both exercises but troops were not briefed accordingly. Safety assumption An MoD inquiry into the potential exposure found no evidence the marines and soldiers had been given a health and protection brief informing them of the asbestos hazard before, during or immediately after deployment. It noted that exercise planners were aware of the asbestos presence. However, questions were not asked about the state of the asbestos or to verify the host nation's claim buildings identified as safe from asbestos were indeed safe. The panel said the "asbestos risk associated with Skrunda-1 had not been correctly identified" and concluded there had been "insufficient reconnaissance and an assumption of safety". A report dated 4 June 2018, as SS18 in Skrunda-1 began, identified the presence of asbestos at the site. A second military plan from April 2019 also stated, in bold, that asbestos was in the buildings - 12 weeks before BP19 arrived. The MoD said: "Action has been taken following a service inquiry into the circumstances surrounding this potential exposure to prevent similar issues arising in the future, and Army use of the Skrunda-1 site is prohibited." Image caption, Former Royal Marine Ed Hill logged the complaint against the MoD in August 2019 after collecting his own sample of the dust from Latvia and bringing it back to the UK for testing A BBC investigation revealed Canadian experts found loose asbestos in Skrunda-1 after Latvian claims it had been removed. The testing in June 2022 reportedly found Chrysotile asbestos in 10% of its samples - the same type of loose asbestos fibre claimed to be in the sample collected by Hill. The Canadian Department for Defense banned its troops from working there in 2018. Image caption, One of the accommodation areas within Skrunda-1 used during Exercise Baltic Protector While the MoD is subject to the Health and Safety at Work Act in Great Britain, it is exempt from criminal prosecution because of Crown privilege. , external The Health and Safety at Work Act does not apply to the MoD in its work overseas. The MoD said it applied UK health and safety standards so far as practicable overseas, where local standards fall below UK requirements. Hill, who served for 15 years in the Royal Marines and is now an independent councillor, said he wanted a change to the law. "I'd like the law to change so that the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) has jurisdiction over the health and safety of UK service personnel wherever they serve in the world," he said. The settlement allows a return for further damages should any of those in the claim go on to develop asbestos-related diseases. The group said it previously asked that 70 unidentified personnel, who were also in Skrunda-1, be informed of the possible exposure. They claim the MoD rejected the request. A second claim from a further 55 service personnel relating to the two Latvian exercises is ongoing. It is understood they were identified too late to join the existing claim. In response to the service inquiry's recommendations, it is understood the MoD has updated its policy on managing asbestos. Asbestos compensation Asbestos is made up of microscopic fibres. When disturbed, it can be inhaled which can cause serious diseases and cancer, like diffuse mesothelioma. Veterans diagnosed with diffuse mesothelioma have a choice of a lump sum compensation of Â£185,000, which was increased in April from Â£140,000, or a monthly payment. Since 2016, the government has paid military veterans diagnosed with mesothelioma more than Â£125m in lump sum compensation. Â£13.4m of that was paid in the last tax year. It is thought, due to short life expectancy, that many veterans opt for the lump sum. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cje3.text: Image source, Embassy of India in Israel Image caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage" By Henry Moore ,Â in London, Â and Â Soutik Biswas ,Â India correspondent ,Â Reporting from in Delhi Published 1 October 2026 The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar. Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia. The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia. The Indian embassy in the United Arab Emirates said Machchhar was "in good health and recovering well". Ambassador Deepak Mittal said he was "proud of Capt Smit for his bravery" and "very reassured" to meet him. Netanyahu wrote on X that Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster". Years of experience Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022 as an experienced pilot. Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, told the BBC he remembered Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis. "We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker." Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile. His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives". An old friend who worked with him at SpiceJet, Capt Dharav Gosalia, described him as outgoing and "very jovial" . Machchhar - whose nickname was "Smit Mac" - was a "disciplined flier" who had undergone years of training, he said, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who had moved into commercial aviation. Image source, Dharav Gosalia Image caption, Gosalia (left) and Machchhar (right) have known each other since they were 20 Last year, Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter. Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work for his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]", he added. Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family. "Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised. He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely. "In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations. At the time of the conversation, Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had needed to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues that had caused delays. He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want." Indian social media has been awash with praise for Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral. What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel Published 13 hours ago Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022 Stabbed mid-flight Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel. The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli. Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21. Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking. At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing. Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700. Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots. But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane. He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing". The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data. The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Machchhar. Modi and Trump praise Machchhar Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured. "His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery. Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger". US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack. "Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open." Photograph: Carly Earl/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An Aboriginal woman who gave birth via caesarean section to a premature baby has been ‘shackled on and off since she came into the hospital’, says Debbie Kilroy of Sisters Inside. Photograph: Carly Earl/The Guardian Prisons Indigenous woman shackled to hospital bed while in labour in Queensland Birth happens days before Labor and Coalition block bill to ban ‘barbaric practice’ of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Tory Shepherd Sat 17 Oct 2026 23.59 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 01.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend, an advocacy group has said. The birth happened just days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a bill to ban the “barbaric practice” of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth . Debbie Kilroy, the chief executive officer of advocacy group Sisters Inside, said an Aboriginal woman who gave birth via caesarean section to a premature baby on the weekend and was still in hospital had been “shackled on and off since she came into the hospital”. Shackling prisoners giving birth should be a last resort – but it’s happening around Australia anyway Read more Hospital staff rang Sisters Inside after trying everything they could to get the shackles removed, she said. “They were even crying because prison staff wouldn’t remove the shackles.” A Queensland corrective services spokesperson said the incident would be reviewed. “ This incident will be subject to an internal review as restraints are only ever to be used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners where necessary to maintain public safety,” the spokesperson said. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Lidia Thorpe, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman and independent senator for Victoria, introduced bills to the Senate this week to ban shackling and to stop children being strip-searched. “[The] people sitting in this room have the power to end these barbaric, inhumane, traumatic and totally unnecessary practices,” Thorpe said. As part of the UN, Australia has signed on to the Bangkok rules on the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”. But the government said this week the criminal justice system was a matter for the states and territories while the Coalition said it understood the intent of the bill but would not support its passage. The Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr broke ranks to say he was “deeply concerned” about the practice and would raise it with the Queensland attorney general. Kilroy said the woman in the Queensland hospital had been “spiralling” before the shackles were removed on Friday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion “As soon as she was shackled her health was deteriorating,” she said. “Mum wasn’t running anywhere, mum wasn’t being violent.” An inquiry into Thorpe’s bill heard about women having one leg and one arm shackled, with only one arm available to hold their newborn. Thorpe said on Friday that “the Albanese government had the opportunity to take a stand against this barbaric practice”. “Instead, they voted to allow it to continue. Not a day later, we hear of another harrowing case,” she said. Thorpe said it was “a joke” for the commonwealth to leave it to states and territories because they “have the constitutional power to establish a national standard and they are choosing not to use it”. “Instead they continue to handball this issue to jurisdictions that have repeatedly failed to stop it,” she said. “How many more women and their babies have to go through this horrific experience before the Albanese government acts?” Explore more on these topics Prisons Indigenous incarceration Indigenous Australians Health Australian politics Queensland news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters
